q: The preventive costs of labour turnover, incurred to keep workers satisfied and discourage them from leaving, include expenditure on:

options.A: Advertising vacancies and interviewing candidates for replacement
options.B: Welfare amenities, medical facilities and safety measures provided to the existing workforce
options.C: Training of the new workers engaged in place of those who left
options.D: Loss of output during the learning period of new workers

q: A 'pseudo' (artificial) profit centre in an organisation is a department which:

options.A: Sells all its output to outside customers in the open market
options.B: Is not permitted to recover even its own costs from other departments
options.C: Keeps no cost records of any kind
options.D: Does not sell to outsiders, but is treated as a profit centre by valuing its output at an agreed transfer price charged to the departments that receive it

q: The industrial engineering method of estimating costs is distinguished by the fact that it:

options.A: Estimates the cost of a product from a physical analysis of the inputs required — materials, labour time and machine time established by work study and engineering specifications — without depending on historical cost records
options.B: Classifies each item in the past accounts as fixed or variable by inspection
options.C: Uses only the highest and the lowest figures from the past accounts
options.D: Adopts the cost figures reported by other firms in the same industry

q: Under the account classification (ledger analysis) method of segregating costs into fixed and variable elements:

options.A: A mathematical line is fitted to a large number of past observations by regression
options.B: The physical quantities of inputs needed for each unit of output are measured by engineers
options.C: Each item of cost in the accounts is examined and classified as wholly fixed, wholly variable or partly variable on the judgement of the accountant, so the result depends heavily on personal judgement
options.D: Only the costs of the current year are used and all past records are destroyed

q: The standing charges of a machine are Rs 18,000 per month and its effective working time is 300 hours per month. Running charges per hour are: depreciation Rs 40, power Rs 35 and repairs Rs 15. The wages of the machine operator, Rs 90 per hour, are to be included in the rate. The composite machine hour rate is:

options.A: Rs 150 per hour
options.B: Rs 240 per hour
options.C: Rs 180 per hour
options.D: Rs 210 per hour

q: Under a contract, the value of work certified is Rs 24,00,000 and the cost of work done but not yet certified is Rs 1,50,000. Cash received from the contractee is Rs 19,20,000 and Rs 90,000 of profit has been kept in reserve in the work-in-progress. The amount at which work-in-progress will be shown in the contractor's balance sheet is:

Plant costing Rs 6,00,000 was issued to a contract site. During the year, plant with a written-down value of Rs 1,10,000 was returned to stores, plant with a written-down value of Rs 40,000 was lost, and depreciation of Rs 45,000 is chargeable on the plant used at the site. The value of plant remaining at the site at the end of the year is:

A goods transport operator's total operating cost for a month is Rs 13,60,000. During the month he carries a charged load of 200 tonnes over a charged distance of 400 km and another charged load of 150 tonnes over a charged distance of 600 km. His cost per commercial tonne-kilometre is:
In the operating costing of a transport undertaking, standing charges are those which:

options.A: Are incurred per kilometre run by the vehicle, such as fuel and tyres
options.B: Accrue with the passage of time whether the vehicle runs or not — such as the vehicle licence fee, insurance, garage rent and the fixed salary of the driver
options.C: Are incurred only when the vehicle meets with an accident
options.D: Are recovered directly from the passengers as fare

q: On physical verification, a shortage of material in the stores is found to be far in excess of the normal limits of evaporation and handling loss, and enquiry traces it to theft and breakage. In the cost accounts, this shortage should be treated as:

options.A: A normal loss, absorbed by inflating the issue price of the material
options.B: A part of the factory overheads of the period, spread over all jobs
options.C: A personal charge recoverable in full from every worker in the stores
options.D: An abnormal loss, charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account and excluded from the cost of production

q: A material is purchased at Rs 200 per unit. In storage, 20% of the quantity is normally lost by dryage, leaving only the balance fit for issue. Under the inflated price method, the price at which issues should be charged so that the whole purchase cost is recovered from the good quantity is:

options.A: Rs 250 per unit
options.B: Rs 200 per unit
options.C: Rs 240 per unit
options.D: Rs 260 per unit

q: The opening stock of a material is 400 units at Rs 15 per unit. An issue of 250 units is made. Thereafter, 600 units are received at Rs 19 per unit. Under the weighted average method (moving average), the price at which the next issue will be charged is:

options.A: Rs 17.40 per unit
options.B: Rs 19.00 per unit
options.C: Rs 18.20 per unit
options.D: Rs 15.00 per unit

q: In the Theory of Constraints, non-bottleneck resources are deliberately allowed to retain some protective (idle) capacity because:

options.A: Idle capacity at every resource must always be eliminated to raise profit
options.B: A non-bottleneck run continuously at full capacity only piles up work-in-progress before the bottleneck, without increasing the output of the system as a whole
options.C: Working every resource at full capacity raises the throughput of the factory in the same proportion
options.D: Protective capacity is needed so that workers can be paid overtime regularly

q: In throughput accounting, work-in-progress and finished goods inventory are valued for internal reporting at:

options.A: Full absorption cost, including direct labour and all factory overheads
options.B: Prime cost, including direct material and direct labour
options.C: Standard cost, including a share of fixed overheads at the normal capacity rate
options.D: Totally variable cost only — in practice the direct material cost contained in them — with all other conversion costs treated as operating expenses of the period

q: Under the traditional (economic conformance) model of quality costs, the optimum level of quality is the point at which:

options.A: The total quality cost is minimised, where the rising costs of prevention and appraisal just balance the falling costs of internal and external failure — a point which, on this view, tolerates some defects; the total quality management approach disputes this and aims at zero defects
options.B: Prevention and appraisal costs are reduced to zero
options.C: No unit produced is ever defective, whatever the cost of achieving it
options.D: External failure costs are at their highest level

q: Budgeted fixed overheads are Rs 4,00,000 for a budgeted output of 20,000 units. Actual output is 21,000 units and the actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 4,35,000. The total fixed overhead (cost) variance is:

options.A: Rs 35,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 20,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 15,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 15,000 (Favourable)

q: The budgeted sales of a product are 7,500 units at the standard selling price of Rs 64 per unit. The actual quantity sold is 8,200 units. The sales volume variance, computed on the value (turnover) basis at the standard price, is:

options.A: Rs 44,800 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 44,800 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 5,24,800 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 7,00,000 (Favourable)

q: In responsibility accounting, whether a particular cost is controllable by a manager depends on:

options.A: Nothing but the size of the amount involved
options.B: The level of management at which the question is judged and the length of the period considered — a cost that is fixed and uncontrollable for a junior manager in the short run may be controllable at a higher level or over a longer period
options.C: Whether the cost is recorded in the cost ledger or the financial ledger
options.D: Whether the cost happens to be a fixed cost or a variable cost

q: The profit of a firm under marginal costing is Rs 1,20,000. Its opening stock is 2,000 units and its closing stock is 3,500 units, the fixed overhead absorption rate being Rs 6 per unit. The profit under absorption costing is:
A practical limitation of inter-firm comparison as a technique of cost control is that:

options.A: Differences in costing methods, product mix, scale and operating conditions among the member firms can make the compiled averages misleading for any one firm, unless uniform costing is followed
options.B: It requires no secrecy regarding the cost data supplied by the member firms
options.C: It is useful only for comparing the selling prices of the member firms
options.D: It can be carried out meaningfully even when the member firms follow widely different costing methods and produce dissimilar products under dissimilar conditions, because the figures remain fully comparable

q: Under the Adjusted Present Value (APV) method of project appraisal, the value of a project is arrived at by:

options.A: Discounting the project's cash flows at the risk-free rate and adding a risk premium to the result
options.B: Taking the net present value of the project as if it were financed entirely by equity and adding the present value of the financing side effects, such as the tax shield on debt
options.C: Taking the net present value computed at the weighted average cost of capital and deducting the issue costs of the securities raised
options.D: Discounting the project's cash flows at the internal rate of return and adding the terminal value

q: The certainty-equivalent method and the risk-adjusted discount rate method both provide for risk in project appraisal, but they differ in that:

options.A: The certainty-equivalent method adjusts the discount rate, while the risk-adjusted rate method adjusts the cash flows
options.B: The certainty-equivalent method can be used only for government projects, while the other method is confined to private projects
options.C: The certainty-equivalent method adjusts the expected cash flows themselves (the numerator) and discounts them at the risk-free rate, while the risk-adjusted rate method leaves the cash flows unadjusted and raises the discount rate (the denominator)
options.D: The risk-adjusted rate method ignores risk altogether, while the certainty-equivalent method measures it statistically

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 6,00,000 and has a Net Present Value of (+) Rs 34,000 at a discount rate of 10%. It is expected to yield a uniform net cash inflow at the end of each of the next 4 years (cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% = 3.170). The uniform annual net cash inflow is:

A project is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 80,000 at the end of each of Year 3, Year 4 and Year 5, and nothing in Years 1 and 2. The present value factors at 10% are 0.751 for Year 3, 0.683 for Year 4 and 0.621 for Year 5. The present value of these inflows is:
In a DCF appraisal, a perpetual annual saving has been capitalised at Rs 7,50,000. If the saving is Rs 60,000 a year, the rate at which it has been capitalised is:
A project costing Rs 5,40,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,50,000 in Year 1 and Rs 1,80,000 in Year 2, and its payback period works out to exactly 3 years. The net cash inflow in Year 3 is:
A sum invested today at 10% compound interest accumulates to Rs 2,66,200 at the end of 3 years (future value factor for 3 years at 10% = 1.331). The sum originally invested is:
By the 'rule of 72', money invested at a compound rate of 8% per annum will double itself in approximately:

options.A: 7.2 years
options.B: 9 years
options.C: 10 years
options.D: 12 years

q: A project has an initial outlay of Rs 11,00,000 and the present value of its cash inflows is Rs 14,00,000, giving a Net Present Value of (+) Rs 3,00,000. If the cash inflows turn out to be 10% lower than estimated, the outlay remaining unchanged, the revised Net Present Value will be:

A project has a Net Present Value of (+) Rs 1,50,000 and the present value of its cash inflows is Rs 10,00,000. Its switching value in respect of the cash inflows, i.e., the maximum percentage by which the inflows can fall before the Net Present Value becomes zero, is:

A new machine costing Rs 7,00,000 will replace an old machine which can be sold at once for Rs 1,00,000. The replacement will yield net cash savings of Rs 1,80,000 at the end of each of the next 4 years (cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% = 3.170). The incremental Net Present Value of the replacement, and the correct decision, are:

options.A: (+) Rs 29,400; the replacement should be accepted
options.B: (-) Rs 5,70,600; the replacement should be rejected
options.C: (-) Rs 29,400; the replacement should be rejected
options.D: (+) Rs 6,00,000; the replacement should be accepted

q: The expected net cash inflow of a project in a year is Rs 2,40,000 and its coefficient of variation is 0.25. The standard deviation of the inflow is:

A company issues 10% debentures of Rs 100 each at Rs 95 per debenture, redeemable after 5 years at Rs 105 per debenture. Using the approximation [annual interest + (redemption value - net proceeds) / years] / [(redemption value + net proceeds) / 2], the approximate cost of the debentures before tax is:
The Profitability Index, though reliable for ranking divisible projects under a funds constraint, can mislead when two mutually exclusive projects of very different size are compared, because it:

options.A: Measures the return per rupee invested and not the total addition to wealth, so a small project may show the higher index while adding far less in absolute terms
options.B: Ignores the time value of money altogether
options.C: Cannot be computed when the net present value is negative
options.D: Always favours the larger of the two projects

q: Two projects have the same cost and the same total depreciation over their lives, but in one the depreciation is charged on the written-down-value basis and in the other on the straight-line basis. The present value of the depreciation tax shield will be higher for the written-down-value project because:

options.A: The total depreciation charged under that method is larger
options.B: Depreciation under that method is not subject to tax
options.C: Larger depreciation, and hence a larger tax saving, arises in the earlier years, and earlier cash savings discount to a higher present value
options.D: The written-down-value method lengthens the life of the project

q: A proposal involves receiving a large sum at the outset and incurring cash outflows in the later years (a financing-type, or borrowing-type, flow pattern, the reverse of an ordinary investment project). For such a proposal, the internal rate of return rule works in reverse, in that the proposal is worthwhile when:

options.A: Its internal rate of return is the highest among the alternatives
options.B: Its internal rate of return is lower than the cost of capital, since the rate here is in effect a cost of the funds obtained
options.C: Its internal rate of return is exactly equal to its payback reciprocal
options.D: It has no internal rate of return at all

q: In the economic appraisal of a project in an economy with surplus unskilled labour, the wages payable to such labour are valued not at the market wage but at a lower 'shadow wage', because the shadow wage represents:

options.A: The minimum wage fixed by statute for the region
options.B: The wage after deducting income tax
options.C: The wage that would be paid if the labour were imported from another region
options.D: The true economic (opportunity) cost of the labour to the economy, which is low because the workers would otherwise produce little or nothing

q: In appraising a project, the cash flows have been estimated at constant (today's) prices, i.e., in real terms, but they are discounted at the nominal (money) rate of return, which includes an allowance for inflation. The result of this mismatch will be that the computed Net Present Value is:

options.A: Understated, so that a worthwhile project may wrongly be rejected
options.B: Overstated, so that an unprofitable project may wrongly be accepted
options.C: Unaffected, because the two errors cancel out
options.D: Exactly equal to the internal rate of return of the project

q: In a lease-versus-buy appraisal, the lease rentals are usually discounted at the after-tax cost of debt rather than at the general cost of capital, because:

options.A: Lease rentals are always smaller than the purchase price of the asset
options.B: Leasing does not involve any cash outflow
options.C: Lease obligations are fixed, contractual and debt-like in nature, so the borrowing rate reflects their risk appropriately
options.D: The lessor bears the whole risk of ownership of the asset

q: A drawback of judging a project by its benefit-cost ratio, as compared with its net present value, is that the ratio:

options.A: Cannot be computed from discounted figures
options.B: Changes according to whether an item is treated as a benefit or as a reduction of cost, although the net present value remains the same either way
options.C: Is always less than 1 for a socially desirable project
options.D: Ignores the initial outlay of the project

q: In social cost-benefit appraisal, the practice of applying 'distribution weights' to a project's costs and benefits means that:

options.A: All costs and benefits are divided equally among the years of the project's life
options.B: The costs of the project are distributed among the departments that use its output
options.C: Benefits are valued at world prices rather than at domestic prices
options.D: A rupee of benefit accruing to a poorer section of society is given a higher weight than a rupee accruing to a richer section, so that the project's effect on income distribution enters the appraisal

q: An enterprise has an inventory holding period of 85 days and a receivables collection period of 45 days, and its cash conversion cycle is 55 days. Its payables deferral (payment) period is:

options.A: 40 days
options.B: 55 days
options.C: 75 days
options.D: 130 days

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 21,60,000 and its inventory turnover ratio is 8 times. Its opening inventory is Rs 2,30,000. Its closing inventory is:
The sales of an enterprise are Rs 16,00,000 and its gross profit ratio is 25%. Its cost of goods sold is:
The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 9,60,000 and its interest coverage ratio is 6 times. The interest payable by it is:
The sales of an enterprise are Rs 36,00,000 and its total assets turnover ratio is 2.4 times. Its total assets are:
The equity shareholders' funds of a company are Rs 24,00,000 and the book value per share is Rs 120. The number of equity shares of the company is:
A company has Earnings Per Share of Rs 24 and a dividend payout ratio of 35%. Its Dividend Per Share is:
A company declares a Dividend Per Share of Rs 14 and the dividend yield on its share is 8%. The market price of the share is:

options.A: Rs 14
options.B: Rs 175
options.C: Rs 112
options.D: Rs 196

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 7,20,000 and its Return on Capital Employed is 18%. Its capital employed is:
The annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 25,55,000 and its creditors turnover ratio is 7 times. Its average trade creditors are:
On the DuPont decomposition, an enterprise earns a return on assets of 12% and its total assets turnover is 1.5 times. Its net profit margin is:
Where the operating ratio is expressed as operating cost divided by net sales, the operating ratio and the operating profit ratio of the same enterprise for the same period always add up to:

options.A: The gross profit ratio
options.C: The net profit ratio

q: An enterprise whose net working capital is negative is one in which:

options.A: It has no current assets at all
options.B: Its fixed assets are financed entirely out of long-term funds
options.C: Its current liabilities exceed its current assets, so that a part of its long-term assets is in effect financed out of short-term liabilities
options.D: Its current ratio is exactly 2 : 1

q: In ratio analysis, a proprietary ratio computed at more than 1 (i.e., proprietors' funds exceeding total assets) is:

options.A: Impossible in a correctly drawn-up balance sheet, since the proprietors' funds are only one part of the total liabilities that equal the total assets, and such a figure points to an error in the computation
options.B: A sign of an exceptionally strong enterprise
options.C: Normal for an enterprise that has no outside liabilities
options.D: Possible whenever the enterprise has large reserves

q: An enterprise collects Rs 1,00,000 in cash from its trade debtors. The immediate effect of this collection on its current ratio and its quick ratio is that:

options.A: Both ratios improve
options.B: Both ratios deteriorate
options.C: The current ratio improves but the quick ratio is unchanged
options.D: Both ratios remain unchanged, because one current (and liquid) asset is merely replaced by another of the same amount

q: A company issues new equity shares wholly for cash. The immediate effect of the issue on its ratios is that:

options.A: Its debt-equity ratio rises and its proprietary ratio falls
options.B: Its debt-equity ratio falls and its proprietary ratio rises
options.C: Both ratios remain unchanged
options.D: Its debt-equity ratio falls but its proprietary ratio also falls

q: A company converts a part of its debentures into equity shares. Its profit before interest and tax remaining unchanged, the immediate effect on its interest coverage ratio is that the ratio:

options.A: Falls, because the equity base has increased
options.B: Remains unchanged, because the total capital is unchanged
options.C: Improves, because the interest charge to be covered has become smaller
options.D: Becomes zero, because there is no longer any debt

q: An enterprise raises a long-term loan and, for the present, keeps the whole amount as a bank balance. The immediate combined effect is that:

options.A: Its current ratio improves, but its debt-equity ratio worsens
options.B: Its current ratio worsens, but its debt-equity ratio improves
options.C: Both ratios improve
options.D: Both ratios worsen

q: An enterprise earns a Return on Capital Employed of 8% but borrows additional funds at 12% per annum and employs them in the same business. The effect of this borrowing on its Return on Equity will be to:

options.A: Raise it above the Return on Capital Employed
options.B: Leave it exactly equal to the Return on Capital Employed
options.C: Raise it, because total capital employed has increased
options.D: Pull it down, because the enterprise pays more for the borrowed funds than it earns on them

q: The fixed charge coverage ratio is a wider measure of debt-servicing capacity than the interest coverage ratio because, besides interest, it also takes into account:

options.A: The depreciation charged on fixed assets
options.B: Other fixed obligations such as lease rentals and the repayment of principal (or sinking fund appropriation)
options.C: The dividend payable on equity shares
options.D: The tax payable on the profits of the enterprise

q: In computing turnover ratios, average balances of debtors, creditors and stock are preferred to the balances on the closing date mainly because:

options.A: Closing balances are never available to the analyst
options.B: Average balances are always larger than closing balances
options.C: The numerator of such a ratio is a flow spread over the whole period, so the denominator should likewise represent the amount typically held during that period and not merely on one day
options.D: The Companies Act requires ratios to be computed on averages

q: A ratio, being a relative measure, can conceal the absolute size of the enterprise, so that:

options.A: A small enterprise and a large enterprise may show the identical ratio although the amounts involved, and hence the significance of the position, differ greatly
options.B: Ratios can never be compared between two enterprises
options.C: Ratios are of no use in inter-firm comparison
options.D: Absolute figures are always preferable to ratios for every purpose

q: In the inventory turnover ratio, the cost of goods sold is used in the numerator in preference to sales mainly because:

options.A: Sales figures are not recorded in the accounts
options.B: The cost of goods sold is always larger than sales
options.C: The ratio is required to be expressed as a percentage
options.D: Sales include a profit element, whereas the inventory in the denominator is valued at cost, so using cost in both keeps the two figures on a consistent basis

q: The ratios of an enterprise which carries on a highly seasonal business, computed from its balance sheet drawn up at the end of its slack season, are liable to mislead mainly because:

options.A: Seasonal businesses are exempt from preparing a balance sheet
options.B: The stock and debtor balances on that single date are far below the levels carried during most of the year, so the picture they give is not representative of the year as a whole
options.C: Ratios cannot be computed for a seasonal business
options.D: Its current liabilities are always nil at the end of the slack season

q: Under line-item (object-of-expenditure) budgeting, expenditure is classified primarily according to:

options.A: The programmes and activities to be carried out
options.B: The objects or inputs on which money will be spent, such as salaries, supplies and equipment
options.C: The outputs and results to be achieved
options.D: The organisational units ranked by priority of need

q: The principal weakness of incremental budgeting is that it:

options.A: Requires every activity to be justified afresh from a zero base each year
options.B: Cannot be used for more than one budget period at a time
options.C: Carries forward existing activities and any inefficiency embedded in them without fresh scrutiny, merely adjusting the previous year's figures
options.D: Is applicable only to capital expenditure and not to revenue expenditure

q: The production budget of a manufacturing enterprise is expressed primarily in:

options.A: Physical units of output to be produced
options.B: Rupees of budgeted production cost
options.C: Standard labour hours of work
options.D: Machine hours of plant utilisation

q: In preparing the sales budget, which of the following is an external factor beyond the control of the enterprise?

options.A: The productive capacity of its plant
options.B: The pricing policy adopted by the enterprise
options.C: The sales force employed by the enterprise
options.D: The intensity of competition and general market conditions

q: Budgets are broadly divided into operating budgets and financial budgets. Which of the following is a financial budget?

options.A: Sales budget
options.B: Cash budget
options.C: Production budget
options.D: Materials purchase budget

q: A recognised drawback of participative (bottom-up) budgeting is that it:

options.A: Tends to become a slow, time-consuming process of negotiation and may allow managers to build slack into their estimates
options.B: Destroys all commitment of managers to the budget targets
options.C: Can be applied only where standard costing is in operation
options.D: Makes it impossible to consolidate the budgets of different departments

q: A cash budget is normally drawn up for short intervals, such as months subdivided into weeks, mainly in order to:

options.A: Match the period covered by the capital expenditure budget
options.B: Keep a close and continuous watch on the liquidity position and arrange finance in time
options.C: Avoid the need for preparing a master budget
options.D: Ensure that depreciation is charged evenly over the year

q: Under the projected balance sheet method of preparing a cash budget, the budgeted closing cash balance is obtained as:

options.A: The total of the receipts side of the cash book
options.B: The difference between budgeted receipts and budgeted payments
options.C: The balancing figure of the projected balance sheet, after all other assets and liabilities have been estimated
options.D: A fixed percentage of the budgeted sales for the period

q: The budgeted total cost of a department is Rs 2,10,000 at 70% capacity and Rs 2,50,000 at 90% capacity, cost varying evenly with capacity between these levels. The budgeted total cost at 80% capacity will be:

A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 40,000, estimated receipts of Rs 2,60,000 and estimated payments of Rs 3,45,000. The enterprise must maintain a minimum cash balance of Rs 25,000 at all times. The borrowing it must arrange for the month is:

An enterprise pays wages 80% in the month in which they are incurred and the remaining 20% in the following month. Wages were Rs 60,000 in March and are budgeted at Rs 75,000 in April. The cash payment for wages budgeted in April is:
A newly established enterprise has no past records on which to base its budgets. Its budgets will have to be built up mainly from:

options.A: The previous year's figures increased by a suitable percentage
options.B: The budgets of the largest competitor, copied without change
options.C: A fixed percentage of its share capital laid down in advance
options.D: Market surveys, industry norms and fresh estimates made from scratch

q: The cost of production budget of a manufacturing enterprise primarily shows:

options.A: The cash required for purchasing raw materials during the period
options.B: The total budgeted cost of the planned output, by combining the materials, labour and overhead budgets
options.C: The budgeted profit on the goods expected to be sold
options.D: The selling and distribution expenses of the planned sales

q: The credit sales of an enterprise for a month are Rs 2,00,000. Half of the customers pay within the month of sale and avail a cash discount of 2%; the other half pay in full in the following month. The cash collected during the month of sale, in respect of that month's credit sales, is:
The transaction motive for holding cash means holding cash in order to:

options.A: Meet the day-to-day payments arising in the normal course of business, such as wages, purchases and expenses
options.B: Provide against unforeseen emergencies such as a breakdown or a flood
options.C: Take advantage of a sudden fall in the prices of materials or securities
options.D: Satisfy the minimum balance condition imposed by the lending bank

q: The speculative motive for holding cash means holding cash in order to:

options.A: Pay wages and salaries on the due dates
options.B: Meet an unexpected demand for repayment by a creditor
options.C: Take advantage of unexpected favourable opportunities, such as a bargain purchase of materials or a rise in interest rates for investing surplus funds
options.D: Maintain the compensating balance required under a loan agreement

q: The Chore Committee on working capital finance recommended that the cash credit limit of a borrower be bifurcated into:

options.A: A fixed deposit component and a current account component
options.B: A core loan component and a fluctuating demand cash credit component
options.C: A rupee component and a foreign currency component
options.D: A secured component and a clean (unsecured) component

q: For seasonal industries, the Chore Committee recommended, in addition to bifurcation of the cash credit limit, that banks should fix:

options.A: A single uniform limit for the whole year, without any variation
options.B: Limits only for the peak season, leaving the borrower to manage otherwise
options.C: No limit at all, finance being given only against bills
options.D: Separate peak-level and non-peak-level limits, supported by quarterly operating plans and statements from the borrower

q: An enterprise is said to have a negative operating (cash conversion) cycle when:

options.A: It collects cash from its customers before the corresponding payments to its suppliers fall due, so that supplier credit finances its operations
options.B: Its current liabilities are exactly equal to its current assets
options.C: It holds no inventory of any kind during the year
options.D: Its sales are made wholly for cash and its purchases wholly on credit of one week

q: Under hypothecation, as a mode of charging stocks for bank finance of working capital:

options.A: The goods are physically handed over to the bank and stored in the bank's godown
options.B: Ownership of the goods passes to the bank until the advance is repaid
options.C: The goods remain in the possession and ownership of the borrower, the bank having only a charge over them with a right to take possession on default
options.D: The borrower merely gives a personal guarantee and no charge is created on the stocks

q: Under the key loan system of advance against stocks:

options.A: The borrower keeps the stocks in his own godown without any control by the bank
options.B: The stocks are stored in a godown under the lock and key of the bank and are released to the borrower only against payment
options.C: The bank advances money only against the personal security of the proprietor
options.D: The stocks are sold by the bank immediately on the advance being made

q: Where the working capital requirement of a borrower is large and is financed jointly by several banks under a consortium arrangement, the banks generally share:

options.A: An exclusive charge, each bank over a separate godown of the borrower
options.B: No charge at all, the advance being treated as clean
